extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IP litigators, judges, and legal advisors working on Brazilian patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing patent litigation in Brazil, including jurisdiction and court organization, types of actions (infringement, nullity, damages), infringement analysis, defenses, criminal provisions, and case-management rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court organization and jurisdiction for patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases related to patent infringements can be filed before any of the trial courts that make up the state courts, ... Any trial court can accept such cases as long as the criteria for the definition of jurisdiction are observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trial courts handle first-instance (single judge) matters and appeals go to panels in appellate courts; exceptional review by the STJ (federal law issues) or STF (constitutional issues). Judicial workload determines number and specialization of courts; resolutions of state/regional federal courts regulate jurisdiction distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized intellectual property judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial courts to which patent cases are assigned are not specialized in Brazil, except where the patent caseload justifies specialization (e.g., São Paulo State Court, Rio Grande do Sul appellate instance, Federal Court of the 2nd Region).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialization may exist at first and appellate instances in particular jurisdictions; specialized chambers judge corporate/intellectual property/business matters. No courts have exclusive jurisdiction over patent issues nationwide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of patent-related actions and standing to sue
rubrics_metrics.description: Main actions: action for prohibition; action for damages; invention patent claim action; action for patent nullity; action for a writ of mandamus; provisional remedies; criminal action (usually private initiative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standing differs by action: e.g., holder of the industrial property right sues in prohibition; patent holder/successors/assignees can sue for damages; inventor can bring patent claim action if usurped; any person with legitimate interest may file nullity; INPI is indispensable defendant in nullity actions filed in federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent nullity grounds and remedies (Article 46 LPI and Articles 46–49)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is null if granted while violating legal provisions (Article 46 of the LPI). Nullity may be argued at any time as a defense and may be sought administratively or judicially (Articles 46–49).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nullity actions are filed before federal courts and, if granted, produce ex tunc (retroactive) and erga omnes (binding on everyone) effects from the application filing. INPI must be ordered to nullify and record annulment under Article 57 LPI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of the Patent Law Treaty on formal defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 10 of the Patent Law Treaty forbids invalidation of a patent for noncompliance with formal requirements if there is no fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brazil has signed but not ratified the treaty; therefore Article 46 LPI's broad scope (including formal/procedural noncompliance) remains applicable domestically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural features of nullity actions (federal jurisdiction, INPI involvement, timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nullity actions require INPI as a defendant and are filed in federal courts; Article 57(1) establishes a 60-day term for the defendant to submit an answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judge may provisionally suspend patent effects under Article 300 CPC if requested (requires periculum in mora and fumus boni iuris). Nullity can be argued as defense; procedural interaction with state-level infringement cases raises issues of external priority and suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between invalidity and infringement proceedings (external priority and incidental nullity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nullity may be argued incidentally as a defense (Article 56(1)), but federal jurisdiction of INPI often prevents state courts from deciding nullity; external priority can suspend infringement cases under Article 313(V) CPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: STJ case law has evolved: earlier it barred incidental nullity in state courts, but more recently allowed incidenter tantum examination of patent nullity in infringement suits (waiving INPI participation), raising open questions on evidence sharing and suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement analysis based on claim scope (Article 41 LPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine infringement, verify whether the accused product/process has all the characteristics of a patent's independent claims; independent claims define essential characteristics and dependent claims help interpret terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims don't limit scope but clarify terms; use dependent claims to detect infringement and see if infringement extends to narrower dependent claim terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct (literal) infringement (Article 42 LPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct or literal infringement occurs when each element of the infringing product coincides with the definition contained in the claim. Patent holder may prevent third parties from producing, using, selling, importing, etc., the patented product or processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of claim expressions may be needed; once meaning established, correspondence is immediate. Protection covers both product and 'process or product obtained directly through a patented process'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal provisions for infringement (Articles 184–186 LPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 184 defines crimes against patented inventions/utility models (e.g., export, sell, import products whose manufacture infringes a patent). Article 185 penalizes supplying components/materials if final application necessarily entails exploitation of the patent. Article 186 states crimes are characterized even if infringement does not reach all claims or is by equivalent means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal liability is distinct from civil liability; penalties include imprisonment or fines. Criminal provisions indicate that equivalent means can ground criminal characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof reversal for process patents (Article 42(2) LPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: A process patent is infringed when the processor fails to prove that their product was obtained by a manufacturing process other than that protected by the patent; this reverses the burden of proof onto the alleged infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This evidentiary rule facilitates enforcement of process patents by requiring defendants to demonstrate an alternative manufacturing route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect (contributory/inducement) infringement (Article 42(1) and Article 185)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent holders can prevent third parties from contributing to infringing acts by others; criminal Article 185 criminalizes supplying components/materials if final application necessarily entails exploitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurists advise a balanced interpretation: liability should not reach sellers of common spare parts used for non-infringing purposes; contributory infringement may require a showing of inducement or partial contribution to the listed infringing acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement by equivalence is non-literal: an element of an accused product does not fall under the literal claim definition but is a technical equivalent of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence may be direct (extend claim scope) or inverse (restrict claim scope). Limitations include non-extension to subject matter within the state of the art and not recovering protection surrendered during prosecution. Jurists suggest interpreting claims by considering legal meaning, specifications, state of the art, prosecution history, and technical field meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the LPI does not expressly provide for reverse equivalence, jurists hold that restrictive interpretation (reverse equivalence) may be applied when needed to avoid determination of nullity, at the request of the patent holder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a limiting or restrictive interpretation to reconcile validity concerns with alleged infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraterritorial infringement and imports (Article 68 LPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement may be recognized even if the act occurred outside Brazilian territory if an unauthorized third party seeks undue economic advantage; Article 68(4) allows third-party imports of product manufactured according to a protected process/product provided it was placed on the market by the holder or with their consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallel importation can be prevented because Article 43(IV) exhaustion covers only products placed on the domestic market by the holder or with their consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of liability defenses (Articles 43 and 45 LPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles 43 and 45 enumerate situations where a patent is not infringed: private noncommercial acts that don't harm patent holder's economic interests (Article 43(I)); prior good-faith exploitation in Brazil before filing/priority date allows continued exploitation (Article 45).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 45(2) excludes those who learned of subject matter via certain disclosures; Article 45(1) limits assignment of the prior use right to the relevant business/company or representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent or license as a defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Third parties may claim a license or consent authorizing their use of the patent to exempt them from infringement liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If license or authorized placement on market exists, it can negate infringement or trigger exhaustion for that product.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-sale (exhaustion) doctrine (Article 43(IV) LPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhaustion: a product placed on the domestic market by the patent holder or with their consent exhausts the patent holder's rights over that product (Article 43(IV)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhaustion applies to the specific product sold, not the patent as a whole; secondary exploitation may still infringe. For multiple patent holders, check whether any holder had right to place product on market. For living matter, exploitation/sale allowed with limits (no commercial propagation). Exhaustion under the LPI applies only to domestic market placements; patent holders may prevent parallel importation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue, jurisdiction and case assignment rules (CPC provisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When INPI participates (nullity), federal courts have absolute jurisdiction (intuito personae) and the judge must declare it ex officio under penalty of nullity; incidental nullity in state courts does not attract federal jurisdiction. Jurisdiction is determined at filing/assignment (Articles 42–53 CPC; Article 43 CPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brazil distinguishes absolute v. relative jurisdiction: absolute jurisdiction must be checked by judge (Article 64 CPC); relative jurisdiction objections must be raised in the answer (Article 65 CPC). Venue for personal-rights cases is defendant domicile (Article 46 CPC) with special rules for multiple domiciles and foreign defendants. External priority and suspension rules apply under Article 313(V) CPC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction between actions: joinder, connection, suspension and external priority (CPC Articles 55–59, 313–315)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions are 'connected' (continência) where they share common request/cause of action or risk contradictory decisions (Article 55 CPC); joinder happens in court obtaining prevention (Articles 56–59). A case may be suspended if its merits depend on another pending case (Article 313(V) CPC) or if merits depend on criminal proceedings (Article 315 CPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joinder requires none of the cases to have been decided; suspension forbids procedural acts but allows urgent acts; external priority can suspend state infringement proceedings where federal nullity action is pending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bankruptcy interaction with patent litigation (Law No. 11,101 Article 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Declaration of bankruptcy or court-supervised reorganization does not affect processing of actions demanding illiquid amounts or requesting nullity; such actions continue with the judge who would have had jurisdiction absent bankruptcy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a bankrupt company is sentenced for patent infringement, the creditor must file proof of claim in the bankruptcy proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements of case and complaint requirements (Article 2 and Article 141 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispute delimitation is defined by the complaint, the answer, and counterclaims. The complaint must immediately indicate legal theories, factual circumstances and documentary evidence at the first opportunity (Article 2 CPC); judge cannot decide beyond what is requested (Article 141 CPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brazilian procedure does not provide for a pre-judicial evidentiary/construction stage; parties must present their theories and evidence at the initial procedural moments (plaintiff's complaint, defendant's answer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial education and use of experts in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges generally lack specific IP training except in some federal regions (e.g., Regional Federal Appellate Court of the 2nd Region). There is identification of the need for specialized professionals to serve as experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended initiatives: continuous IP training by schools of judges (possibly with INPI collaboration) and preparation of a list of specialized professionals from which judges could choose during evidentiary stages.
